To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a homozygote mutation of Kir6.2 causes neonatal diabetes and that the difference in KATP ATP sensitivity between the homozygote and heterozygote is remarkably small.
a homozygosity for a Kir6.2 mutation causes neonatal diabetes and that tiny differences in Kir6.2 channel activity can have a profound impact on diabetes susceptibility.

a tiny reduction in ATP sensitivity can cause neonatal diabetes and that sulfonylureas are an appropriate treatment for patients with neonatal diabetes caused either by a Kir6.2 mutation or by a SUR1 mutation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how small changes in the activity of the KATP channel can affect the risk of developing diabetes.
the molecular basis of neonatal diabetes and its treatment.
how mutations in genes for KATP channel subunits affect the function of the channel and how these changes affect the function of beta cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a homozygote for a KCNJ11 mutation can develop neonatal diabetes.
the Kir6.G324R variant is associated with a high risk of neonatal diabetes, and that sulfonylureas are a good treatment choice.
homozygosity for the Kir6. 2-G324R variant results in neonatal diabetes, while heterozygosity for the variant does not.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Kir6.G324R mutation is a gain-of-function mutation, whereas Kir6.E23K mutation is a loss-of-function mutation.
the homozygosity of Kir6.2 mutations is not a prerequisite for neonatal diabetes.
tiny changes in Kir6.2 ATP sensitivity markedly affect the risk of diabetes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ATP sensitivity of Kir6.2 is a critical determinant of diabetes risk.
even tiny changes in K(ATP) channel function are sufficient to affect beta cell activity and insulin secretion, and hence diabetes risk.

the risk of developing neonatal diabetes due a heterozygous KCNJ 11 mutation is much lower than previously appreciated, and that the risk of diabetes is further reduced by the presence of a second, wild-type copy of the gene.
